help.title: How to use Chess Trainer
help.intro: Chess Trainer is for practice: drill your openings against a bot that plays your lines, keep playing against Stockfish when theory ends, and review your games. Everything runs and stays on your computer.
help.fairPlay.title: Never use it to cheat
help.fairPlay.text: Do not use Chess Trainer, or any engine, during a game against another person, online or over the board. That is cheating, and Chess.com, Lichess and FIDE ban it. Train before and after your games, never during them.
help.eval.title: The evaluation here is basic
help.eval.text: The evaluation bar and the move icons (best move, mistake, blunder…) come from a quick Stockfish check and are only a hint. For a real analysis, export the PGN and analyze it on Chess.com, Lichess or another analysis tool.
help.start.title: Start a game
help.start.opening: Opening: pick your color and tick the openings and variations to drill. Each ticked variation has the same chance of being drawn. Playing a move from a variation you did not tick counts as leaving theory.
help.start.saved: Saved game: train the line of a game you played or imported, so its moves are checked, or play on from any of its positions.
help.start.chess960: Chess960: roll a starting position or paste the FEN of one of the 960. To castle, click the king and then a square between it and the rook, or the rook itself.
help.start.level: Bot level: the rating beside each level is nominal, on Stockfish's own scale, and has not been measured. It is not a Chess.com or Lichess rating.
help.start.time: Time control: the presets of a real tournament clock, from bullet to classical, or no clock. The bot's response time is Human, which spends its clock like a person, or Instant.
help.start.options: Options: warn when you leave theory, allow premoves, and let the bot deviate from its line on purpose, from a chosen move, so you also train against surprises.
help.play.title: During the game
help.play.moves: Click or drag the pieces. The bot plays the book moves of the drawn line, and when theory ends, or someone leaves it, Stockfish takes over at the chosen level.
help.play.chips: The chips under the board say whose move it is, whether you are still in theory, and where you or the bot left it.
help.play.showMoves: Show moves, in the right bar, hides the opening name and the move list until the end of the game: play without hints, or write the moves on paper.
help.play.premoves: With premoves on, you can queue one move while the bot thinks. With premoves off, Take back undoes your last move while the bot's reply is not shown yet.
help.play.resign: Resign asks for a second click, so a stray click does not end the game.
help.end.title: After the game
help.end.card: The card under the move list shows the result, the variation, how far theory went, and each deviation with the expected move.
help.end.pgn: Copy or download the PGN. New Game starts the next one with the same choices.
help.train.title: How to train
help.train.lose.title: Losing is part of it
help.train.lose.text: Losing is part of learning. What matters is studying each game and learning from your own mistakes. To really improve, raise the bot's level little by little, and only raise it again once you feel comfortable with the moves it plays.
help.train.pace.title: Each time control has a job
help.train.pace.text: In long games, think calmly about every move and build the habit of calculating two, three or more moves ahead. Use rapid, blitz and bullet to drill the patterns you have already taken in.
help.train.threats.title: Start with your opponent's moves
help.train.threats.text: Before each move, first look at what your opponent threatens: checks, captures and attacks. Then look for your own plan.
help.train.board.title: Train as in a tournament
help.train.board.intro: The best way to learn is with a physical board and clock. It does not matter if the clock drifts from the app's.
help.train.board.before: Before the game, open Scoresheet in the menu and print it, or save it as a PDF, and fill in the header. Choose a long time control, such as rapid or classical, and untick Show moves.
help.train.board.move: Move the piece on the board.
help.train.board.press: Press the clock with the same hand that moved the piece.
help.train.board.play: Play the same move in the app.
help.train.board.write: Write the move on the scoresheet.
help.train.board.botPlay: Play its move on the board.
help.train.board.botPress: Press the clock on its side.
help.train.board.botWrite: Write the move on the scoresheet.
help.train.board.botThen: Only then start thinking about yours.
help.train.board.touch: Remember: a piece you touch is a piece you move. For an even better experience, film yourself playing and watch it later to see how you behave at the board. Take your time: with practice it becomes natural.
help.train.board.compare: At the end, fill in the result and the signatures, compare your sheet with the move list and the PGN, and look for the moves you wrote wrong.
help.train.analyse.title: Analyze before you look at the evaluation
help.train.analyse.text: When a game ends, review it on your own first and look for where it turned. Only then check it against the evaluation. The bar shows on the final position, so ignore it until you are done.
help.review.title: Saved games and review
help.review.list: Every game is saved. Search and filter the list, open a game on the board and go through it with the buttons or the arrow keys, Home and End.
help.review.play: Play from here starts a new game from the position on the board.
help.review.export: Tick games to export them as PGN or to delete them.
help.openings.title: Openings
help.openings.browse: Go through every line of the book on the board, and tick lines to export them as PGN.
help.import.title: Import games
help.import.sources: Bring your games from Chess.com or Lichess by username and period, or paste or upload a PGN. They go to Saved Games, ready to review or to train.
help.analyse.title: Analyze elsewhere
help.analyse.export: Get the PGN from the end-of-game card or from Saved Games.
help.analyse.paste: On Chess.com or Lichess, open the analysis board and paste or import the PGN, for a full, deeper analysis.

about.title: About Chess Trainer
about.me.title: Who made it
about.me.text: I am Nielsen Campos: a data and backend engineer, a semi-professional musician (almost amateur) and an amateur chess player (and I think that is where it stops, or maybe not, who knows 😂).
about.project.title: The project
about.project.text: Chess Trainer is a simple place to study for players who teach themselves. It started as a single page to drill my own openings and grew into a place to train in general, to learn without a real instructor and even without playing over the board.
about.project.private: Its advantages: your study stays on your own computer, not online, so your preparation stays private, as grandmasters keep theirs today. Nothing leaves it unless you import your games from a site. And it costs nothing: just run it and use it.
about.project.help: It does not replace courses, learning platforms or instructors. It is only a help for amateur, beginner and semi-professional players.
about.path.title: Who paved my way
about.path.intro: In chronological order, the people, books and platforms that brought me here.
about.mecking: Brazilian grandmaster, once third in the world. I have been learning chess from the book Mequinho: o xadrez de um grande mestre since 1991.
about.chessmaster: The best-selling series of chess video games, today Ubisoft's. I started playing it in 2001, on the SNES and the PC.
about.agadmator: Croatian YouTuber whose channel goes through famous games; in 2021 he was the first chess creator to pass a million subscribers. On his channel I started watching chess and getting to know the great masters, and in 2014 I started playing online.
about.lichess: A free and open-source chess site, with no ads, run by a non-profit. Where I started playing, because of agadmator.
about.levy: American International Master, author and creator, known as "the Internet's chess teacher". I have followed him since 2020. He helped me understand strategy in more depth, get to know the people of the chess world and move to Chess.com for good. His course is on Chessly, and his book is How to Win at Chess.
about.chesscom: The largest chess site in the world. Where I moved because of Levy, and where I kept learning more about chess.
about.evandro: Brazilian grandmaster and creator, with whom I have been learning to plan since 2023, also through his course platform, Chessflix.
about.hikaru: American grandmaster, five-time U.S. champion, 2022 Fischer Random world champion, one of the best players in the world and one of its biggest streamers. I found him through Levy around 2024, and learned a lot from him about memorization. His style reminds me of Tal's, the Magician from Riga.
about.krikor: Brazilian grandmaster and creator, Brazilian champion in 2012 and 2015, who played five Chess Olympiads for Brazil. From him I have been learning tactics since around 2024, also through his courses on openings and more. With WIM Flor, he hosts Chess.com's broadcasts in Portuguese on YouTube.
about.legends.title: Other legends and references
about.legend.botez: Canadian sisters who host BotezLive, one of the best-known chess channels, mixing chess and entertainment. Alexandra is a Woman FIDE Master and played three Women's Chess Olympiads for Canada.
about.legend.anand: Indian, his country's first grandmaster and world champion from 2007 to 2013.
about.legend.fischer: American, world champion from 1972 to 1975 after beating Spassky in the Match of the Century, and the creator of Chess960 (Fischer Random).
about.legend.ivanchuk: Ukrainian grandmaster since 1988, three times number two in the world, known for his creativity and for playing almost any opening.
about.legend.karpov: World champion from 1975 to 1985, and FIDE champion again from 1993 to 1999, famous for his positional play.
about.legend.mamedyarov: Azerbaijani grandmaster and his country's highest-rated player, whose best rating, 2820, is among the highest in history.
about.legend.waitzkin: American chess prodigy, twice U.S. junior champion, whose childhood inspired the film Searching for Bobby Fischer. He later became a martial arts world champion and wrote The Art of Learning.
about.legend.carlsen: Norwegian, world champion from 2013 to 2023 and the highest-rated player in history.
about.legend.fernandez: Argentine Woman International Master (WIM), five-time Argentine women's champion. With Krikor, she hosts Chess.com's broadcasts in Portuguese.
about.legend.kasparov: World champion from 1985 to 2000, and number one in the world for about twenty years.
about.legend.leitao: Brazilian grandmaster, seven-time Brazilian champion, also a correspondence chess grandmaster (ICCF), who teaches on his channel.
about.legend.molina: Brazilian International Master, Brazilian champion in 2018. In 2021 he beat Levy in the final of the I'm Not A GM Speed Chess Championship.
about.legend.naroditsky: In memoriam. American grandmaster, author and commentator, and one of the best chess teachers on YouTube.
about.legend.niemann: American grandmaster since 2021 and streamer, one of the strongest young players of his generation.
about.legend.polgar: Hungarian grandmaster, considered the strongest woman player in history.
about.legend.rosen: American International Master and streamer, known for his traps, the Stafford Gambit and his calm "Oh no, my queen!".
about.legend.supi: Brazilian grandmaster since 2018 and three-time Brazilian champion.
about.legend.tal: World champion in 1960, the Magician from Riga, famous for his sacrifices and attacks.
